name: r3-across-2
statement: The cued base can leave a loop or a wrong line through probable tokens in the head of the distribution, so it does not need untruncated T 1.0. Sharpening (T 0.6, top-p, min-p) keeps that escape mass and loops do not lock. The RL weight change removes, as a roughly constant per-layer push, probable process tokens ('Wait', 'Hmm') and leaves the escape only in low-probability tail tokens. That makes RL, and small doses of its delta, sensitive to temperature and truncation.
scope: Olmo-3-1025-7B base with the cue, Olmo-3.1-7B-RL-Zero-Math, the merges base + a(RL - base), and the base plus the 32 constant per-layer vectors of result-54f212. MATH-500 at T 0.6-1.5 with top-p or min-p truncation, cap 16,384, grader v3. It explains the loop and cap-hit component of the temperature effect, not the content errors (misreads, slips) that remain at T 1.0, and it does not cover hard328 beyond its cap hits.

imports.finding: In Qwen2.5-Math-7B, RL-trained steering vectors close much of the RL gap. The last-layer vector acts as first-token substitution (equivalent to an opening prefix), and the penultimate-layer vector promotes process words over 'solution', apparently to deter premature endings, through the MLP/unembedding path.
imports.how: This supplies the two pieces: the cue reproduces the first-token part, and a constant push away from process words removes the in-distribution escape route that the base keeps in the head of its distribution. The theory then predicts that the constant vectors alone make the base fragile under sharpening.

explains.how: RL's escape tokens sit in the tail of the distribution, so sharpening deletes them and RL would be expected to loop at T 0.6; the small change shows only that the loop share of its errors is small.
At T 0.6 / top-p 0.95 the base's escape mass in the head is kept, so loops that start still end, and the cap hits left are few and come from other causes.
Removing top-p at T 0.6 returns a lot of tail mass; top-p, not temperature, is the main thing that changes the escape.

explains.quote: Truncating the tail at T 1.0 brings loops back
explains.how: min-p and top-p delete only tail tokens that the base does not rely on, so at T 1.0 they leave its escape intact.

explains.quote: T 1.5 + min-p 0.1 removes them (0 loops, 29 cap)
explains.how: A higher temperature flattens the head and pushes the escape tokens below the min-p cut, so the escape route is weakened rather than restored.

explains.quote: RL readout holds Wait/Hmm at 5.64 % of positions vs base 4.56 %
explains.how: RL moves the hold-on tokens down out of the head of the distribution, which is the escape route that is lost under sharpening.

explains.quote: On the 16 cap hits RL's largest gaps are early
explains.how: Where the base runs to the cap, RL's preferred tokens at the largest gaps are not the escape words.

explains.quote: adding ONE constant vector per layer to the base
explains.how: A fixed per-layer push that closes a quarter to a third of the KL is the right form for a push away from process words that does not depend on context.
The push away from hold-on words is constant, not a correction aimed at errors, as a constant vector would be.
Over-dosing the push (a = 1.5) makes the process-word deficit large enough to break coherent endings.

conflicts.quote: Not larger on the 65 RL-only problems.
conflicts.how: If the hold-on push were the escape route behind RL's gains, it should be weaker on the problems RL rescues. It is not, so at T 1.0 the push does not account for the content-error part of the gap.
Weakening escape mass removes loops but adds no accuracy at T 1.0, so escape mass explains the temperature effect, not the 10-point gap to RL.

rival: The rival: the base's T 0.6 failures are low-entropy collapse caused by its weak continuation of its own long context (knowledge-1497e8), and RL fixes them by changing content, not by removing probable escape tokens. Under the rival, adding the 32 constant per-layer vectors (no content change) leaves T 0.6 cap hits near 119. Under this theory they rise by more than half, and the hold-on rate of the cued base stays flat with temperature while RL's rises.

predictions.experiment: Base Olmo-3-1025-7B with the 32 constant per-layer vectors of result-54f212 added to the residual output of each layer (curve_bias-01, mean RL-minus-base layer output), cue, MATH-500 n = 500, T 0.6 / top-p 0.95, cap 16,384, seeds 1,000,000 + i, grader v3, one H100. Count cap hits.
predictions.refuted_by: 130 or fewer cap hits (constant push does not make loops lock under sharpening; base cue has 119).

predictions.experiment: Merged theta(0.25) = base + 0.25(RL - base) with the cue, MATH-500 n = 500, T 0.6 / top-p 0.95, cap 16,384, seeds 1,000,000 + i, grader v3, one H100.
predictions.refuted_by: Score above 425 (the merge keeps nearly all of the 441 it scores at T 1.0, i.e. a quarter-dose is temperature-insensitive) or cap hits below 50.

predictions.experiment: Offline: how the cued base's hold-on rate changes with temperature (T 1.0 vs T 0.6), finished answers only.
predictions.recipe: Files: S3 r4/base_rl-02/out/T1.jsonl (base cue T 1.0) and S3 r3/base-01/out/F_math500.jsonl (base cue T 0.6 / top-p 0.95), keeping rows with sample == 0 only in F_math500. In both, keep rows with cap_hit false. For each kept row count case-sensitive regex matches of \b(Wait|Hmm)\b in text. Rate = (total matches) / (total characters of text) x 10,000, pooled over rows. Statistic: rate(T1) / rate(F_math500 sample 0).
predictions.refuted_by: Ratio above 1.2 or below 0.83: the base's escape words depend on temperature, so they are not in the head of the distribution.

predictions.experiment: Offline: how the RL model's hold-on rate changes with temperature (T 1.0 vs T 0.6).
predictions.recipe: Files: S3 r4/modal_t2-01/t2/T2.jsonl (RL plain T 1.0) and S3 next_n13/s3gate-03/out/rl/rl/math500/generations.jsonl (RL plain T 0.6 / top-p 0.95). Use all rows of both files (no cap filter, since n13 has no checked cap column). Count case-sensitive regex matches of \b(Wait|Hmm)\b in text. Rate = total matches / total characters x 10,000, pooled. Statistic: rate(T2) / rate(n13 RL).
predictions.refuted_by: Ratio below 1.08: RL writes escape words no more often at T 1.0 than at T 0.6, so the escape route does not sit in the tail.

predictions.experiment: Offline: how far a quarter-dose of the RL delta moves the hold-on rate toward RL's.
predictions.recipe: Files: S3 T1.jsonl (base cue, a = 0), iterate-runs abaybektursun-1114-153102-b029/answers.jsonl (theta0.25_cue), abaybektursun-1114-153110-e985/answers.jsonl (rl_cue, a = 1). One row per problem_index (highest attempt if duplicated); keep rows with cap_hit false. Rate = case-sensitive \b(Wait|Hmm)\b matches / total text characters x 10,000, pooled. Statistic: (rate(theta0.25) - rate(T1)) / (rate(rl_cue) - rate(T1)).
predictions.unit: fraction of the base-to-RL hold-on rate change
predictions.refuted_by: Fraction above 0.6 (the hold-on push saturates by a = 0.25 together with accuracy, so the push is what carries the low-dose gain).
